rules.statement: Name management permission scopes `{verb}:{family}`, where the family is a single entity or one of its leaves (for example settings or secrets), rather than one coarse scope covering an entity and all its sub-resources.
rules.why: Fine-grained delegation such as a secrets-only or settings-only manager can only be expressed when scopes go down to the leaves, so operators can define custom roles without code changes.
rules.check: Look for new management endpoints or scope definitions that reuse a broad entity scope for leaf operations (secrets, settings), or scope names that don't follow `{verb}:{family}`.

rules.statement: Authorize an operation on a resource by checking role assignments at that resource node or any of its ancestors (inherited downward), not by checking a global, resource-independent admin claim.
rules.why: Authority is granted at a specific resource (admin of tenant-a but not tenant-b). Type-level roles and instance ownership are one mechanism at different nodes.
rules.check: Look for authorization handlers or checks that grant tenant- or instance-level access based only on a global role claim without matching the target resource or its ancestors, or that build a separate path for ownership.

rules.statement: Keep resource creation and cross-tenant enumeration on the server-root authority, separate from operations on an existing tenant, which are authorized at that tenant's node.
rules.why: Mixing the two either keeps a tenant admin from managing its own tenant or lets it create tenants or list other tenants.
rules.check: Look for endpoints that guard tenant create/list-all and tenant read/update/delete/deactivate with the same scope or policy, or that allow tenant-scoped authority to list across tenants.

rules.statement: Refuse any operation that would remove the last owner of an owned resource.
rules.why: A resource must always have at least one owner. Only higher-level admins can reassign ownership.
rules.check: Look for owner-removal or owner-replacement code that has no guard against leaving the owner set empty.

rules.statement: When a principal creates an ownable resource, automatically assign it the Owner role on that new instance.
rules.why: The creator becomes the owner, which keeps the at-least-one-owner rule true from the moment the resource exists.
rules.check: Look for create paths for ownable resources that persist the resource without also creating an Owner assignment for the calling principal.

rules.statement: Do not let the Owner role grant permission to create new resources. Owners may only read, update, delete and manage the leaves and owners of the instance they own.
rules.why: Creating a resource is a type-level act that needs a tenant-wide scope (or, later, an approval flow), not instance ownership.
rules.check: Look for Owner role definitions or ownership handlers that include create verbs, or create endpoints that accept ownership as enough.

rules.statement: Define role assignments and ownership over an abstract principal identifier, not over a user/subject-specific type.
rules.why: Service principals (clients) will be added later, and that should be an additive change.
rules.check: Look for assignment or ownership models, storage or handlers that hard-code a user/subject id type instead of a general principal reference.
